newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia's federation econ growth 50 pct - World Bank.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia's federation econ growth 50 pct - World Bank.

text.p: Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation has an annual economic growth rate of 50 percent and the trend is likely to stay at a favourable level in the next three years, a World Bank official said on Monday.
"We are seeing a situation of very substantial growth in the (Moslem-Croat) federation, up to 50 percent a year," Rory O'Sullivan, the bank's Sarajevo director, told Reuters.
"And we project this will continue for the next three years, maybe not at such high level. Our basic projection is 35 percent a year," O'Sullivan said.
Foreign assistance in rebuilding the country devastated by a 3 1/2-year war accounts for 80 percent of the growth rate, with donor investment running at $100 million a month, he said.
"We are clearly talking about 50 percent on a very small base, so it's difficult to compare this 50 percent with, say, seven percent of Poland.
"But the point is that it's happening and by the year 2000 they will regain about 70 percent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of the country," he said.
In 1996, Bosnia-Herzegovina saw a rise in GDP to almost $3 billion from $2 billion at the end of 1995, which translates into a rise of $750 per capita of Gross National Product from $500.
The federation's wages rose by 300 percent in 1996 and currently average around 250 German Marks ($145) a month.

Bosnia's other entity, the Serb republic, is lagging behind the federation because the international community has linked foreign economic assistance to Serb compliance with the country's peace accord.

As a result, the Serbs saw only two percent of the estimated $1.2 billion that foreign donors committed to Bosnia's reconstruction in 1996. Wages in the Serb entity are only a third of the federation's average.
"We consider the growth rate to be really quite low in the Serb republic, not reaching anything like the federation levels," O'Sullivan said.
Under terms of the Dayton peace agreement, the federation covers 51 percent of the country and the Serb entity the remaining 49 percent.
The reconstruction money also helped the Moslem-Croat federation's jobless rate to drop from about 80 percent at the end of 1995 to an estimated 50 percent in 1996, O'Sullivan said.
Experts said about 430,000 people of the 875,000 labour force are employed, making for a 52-54 percent jobless rate.
Although the jobs created by donors' funds are not permanent jobs, the country has a chance to build a self-sustainable economy once the foreign aid ceases to flow, O'Sullivan said.
"The challenge is to convert short-term jobs into longer-term jobs over the period of reconstruction," he said.
After the fighting in Bosnia ended in 1995, the international community pledged to commit $5.1 billion for the country's reconstruction over the period of three to four years.
In 1996, $1.7 billion was pledged for reconstruction. Organisers of a fund-raising conference tentatively set for the end of May in Brussels hope to collect $1.4 billion for 1997.
